claim: argus mutants show approximately 600 fewer minutes of total sleep per 24 hr day compared to iso31 controls
source: aus homozygotes showed ~600 fewer minutes of total sleep per 24 hr day compared to iso31 controls (Ryder et al., 2004) controls (p < 0.0001; Figure 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental sleep measurements shown in Figure 1A-B with statistical significance p < 0.0001

claim: argus sleep decrease is primarily driven by inability to sustain sleep, as reflected in a significant decrease in sleep bout duration during both day and night
source: aus sleep decrease was primarily driven by inability to sustain sleep, as reflected in a significant decrease in aus homozygote sleep bout duration during both day and night (p < 0.0001; Figure 1C)
evidence: The claim is supported by sleep bout duration measurements shown in Figure 1C with statistical significance p < 0.0001

claim: argus mutants take a longer time to initiate sleep after lights off at ZT12 than argus heterozygotes or controls
source: Sleep latency analysis showed that aus mutants took a longer time to initiate sleep after lights off at ZT12 than aus heterozygotes or controls (p < 0.01; Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by sleep latency measurements shown in Figure 1E with statistical significance p < 0.01

claim: Activity index is comparable between argus mutants and controls, indicating that argus is not a hyperactive mutant
source: Activity index, locomotor activity per waking minute, was comparable between aus mutants and controls (p > 0.05; Figure 1F), indicating that aus is not a hyperactive mutant.
evidence: The claim is supported by activity index measurements shown in Figure 1F with no significant difference (p > 0.05)

claim: argus heterozygotes show a small decrease in sleep relative to controls, indicating that the argus mutation is slightly dominant
source: aus heterozygotes showed a small decrease in sleep relative to controls (p < 0.001; Figure 1A–B), indicating that the aus mutation is slightly dominant.
evidence: The claim is supported by sleep measurements in heterozygotes shown in Figure 1A-B with statistical significance p < 0.001

claim: Most argus homozygotes (>60%) show robust locomotor activity rhythms, indicating an intact circadian clock
source: Most aus homozygotes ( > 60%) showed robust locomotor activity rhythms, indicating an intact circadian clock (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by circadian rhythm analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: The overt arrhythmia in approximately 30% of argus homozygotes likely stems from the large reduction in sleep
source: Similarly to other short-sleeping mutants, the overt arrhythmia in ~30% of aus homozygotes likely stems from the large reduction in sleep (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Shi et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to other short-sleeping mutants and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: argus homozygotes display longer activity episodes than controls in constant darkness
source: Notably, aus homozygotes displayed longer activity episodes than controls in constant darkness (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), consistent with their short sleep under LD conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by activity episode data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: The argus mutation was localized distal to ebony through classical mapping
source: Recombinant progeny were screened for sleep phenotypes and subjected to classical mapping, localizing aus distal to ebony.
evidence: The claim is supported by classical genetic mapping experiments described in the text

claim: The argus mutation was localized between SNP markers at approximately 19 and 24 Mb
source: We then developed single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) markers through genomic DNA sequencing of aus mutants and the genetic marker line; the aus mutation was localized between SNP markers at ~19 and 24 Mb (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by SNP marker analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: In the approximately 5 Mb region identified by mapping, 622 argus-specific SNPs were found, of which 10 led to amino acid changes in nine open-reading frames
source: In the ~5 Mb region identified by mapping, we found 622 aus-specific SNPs, of which 10 led to amino acid changes in nine open-reading frames (ORFs) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: Pan-neuronal knockdown of cg16791 with nsyb-Gal4 and either of two independent RNAi lines reduces total sleep
source: Both pan-neuronal knockdown manipulations resulted in significant decreases in total sleep compared to RNAi and Nsyb-Gal4> Dicer2 controls (p < 0.01; Figure 2C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by sleep measurements shown in Figure 2C-D with statistical significance p < 0.01

claim: Pan-neuronal knockdown of cg16791 with elav-Gal4 produces a severe sleep reduction comparable to argus/argus mutants
source: Supporting its identity as the aus locus, pan-neuronal knockdown of cg16791 with elav-Gal4> Dicer and cg16791 RNAi#1 produced a severe sleep reduction comparable to aus/aus mutants (p < 0.0001; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by sleep measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B with statistical significance p < 0.0001

claim: cg16791 regulates sleep in adulthood
source: This shows that cg16791 regulates sleep in adulthood.
evidence: The claim is supported by RU486-inducible knockdown experiments showing adult-specific effects on sleep

claim: Actin-GS> Dicer2+ RNAi#2 flies show a robust decrease in sleep compared to controls on RU+ but not on RU-
source: Actin-GS> Dicer2+ RNAi#2 flies showed a robust decrease in sleep compared to RNAi and Actin-GS> Dicer2 controls on RU+; however, there was no difference between genotypes on RU- (p < 0.0001; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by drug-inducible knockdown experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C with statistical significance p < 0.0001

claim: ProDom search of the full-length CG16791 isoform-A reference sequence identified a number of possible transmembrane motifs
source: An unbiased ProDom search of the full-length CG16791 isoform-A reference sequence identified a number of possible transmembrane motifs (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis using ProDom

claim: TMPred assessment of known CG16791 isoforms predicted their best-fit membrane topology with a 5-transmembrane structure
source: A more targeted TMPred assessment of known CG16791 isoforms predicted their best-fit membrane topology with a 5-transmembrane structure, and placed the aus mutations in an internal loop region between transmembrane helices 3 and 4 (Figure 2D; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by TMPred bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: Deep-Loc-1.0 analysis predicted that all CG16791 isoforms are targeted to the cell membrane, and perhaps to some extent the ER/Golgi network
source: A Deep-Loc-1.0 analysis predicted that all CG16791 isoforms are targeted to the cell membrane, and perhaps to some extent the ER/Golgi network, driven predominantly by signal sequences in the C-terminus (Supplementary file 2; Almagro Armenteros et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by Deep-Loc-1.0 bioinformatic analysis

claim: CG16791 isoform-A was isolated from membrane fractions of fly head
source: Our bioinformatic analyses are experimentally supported by the isolation of CG16791 isoform-A from membrane fractions of fly head (Aradska et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental evidence from a cited study

claim: The P-element insertion allele of cg16791 (P1) failed to complement the argus mutant
source: The P1 allele failed to complement the aus mutant. Thus, P1/aus trans-heterozygotes had severely reduced total sleep comparable to aus homozygotes (p < 0.01; Figure 3A)
evidence: The claim is supported by complementation test results shown in Figure 3A with statistical significance p < 0.01

claim: Transheterozygotes of cg16791-KO and argus show a severe reduction in total sleep, similar to argus homozygotes
source: Behavioral analysis showed that total sleep in cg16791KO heterozygotes is comparable to aus heterozygotes, while trans-heterozygotes of cg16791KO and aus showed a severe reduction in total sleep, similar to aus homozygotes (p < 0.0001; Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by sleep measurements shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C with statistical significance p < 0.0001

claim: Homozygous cg16791 knockouts are semi-lethal with 0.59% survival rate
source: As homozygous knockouts were semi-lethal (0.59% survival rate; 2 / 339 flies tested), we could only reliably obtain cg16791KO heterozygotes.
evidence: The claim is supported by survival rate data from knockout experiments

claim: Pan-neuronal induction of either cg16791 short form or full-length form effectively rescues sleep in argus mutants
source: Pan-neuronal (elav-Gal4) induction of either form effectively rescued sleep in aus mutants (p < 0.0001; Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D with statistical significance p < 0.0001

claim: The CG16791FL N-terminus is dispensable for its sleep function
source: This result also suggests that the CG16791FL N-terminus is dispensable for its sleep function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both short and full-length forms rescue sleep

claim: ausP2k-Gal4 drives GFP expression broadly in the fly brain, including peptidergic neurons of the pars intercerebralis, Kenyon cells of the mushroom body, optic lobe neurons and some lateral neurons
source: GFP was expressed broadly in the fly brain, in many cell types including peptidergic neurons of the pars intercerebralis (PI), Kenyon cells of the mushroom body, optic lobe neurons and some lateral neurons (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by GFP expression pattern shown in Figure 4A

claim: P2k-driven argus expression rescues argus/argus short sleep
source: Importantly, P2k-driven aus expression rescued aus/aus short sleep, indicating that P2k-Gal4 recapitulates the sleep-relevant aus expression pattern (p < 0.05; Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 4A with statistical significance p < 0.05

claim: c929-Gal4-driven argus expression in an argus mutant homozygous background partially rescues the short sleep phenotype
source: c929-Gal4-driven aus expression in an aus mutant homozygous background partially rescued the short sleep phenotype (p < 0.05; Figure 4B)
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 4B with statistical significance p < 0.05

claim: argus expression in peptidergic cells contributes to sleep behavior
source: c929-Gal4-driven aus expression in an aus mutant homozygous background partially rescued the short sleep phenotype (p < 0.05; Figure 4B), demonstrating that aus expression in peptidergic cells contributes to sleep behavior.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiment using peptidergic-specific driver shown in Figure 4B

claim: Transheterozygotes for dimmed and argus show a synergistic loss of sleep compared to the respective single heterozygotes
source: Furthermore, transheterozygotes for dimmed (which have impaired neuropeptidergic neuron function, including in the PI) (Hewes, 2003) and aus show a synergistic loss of sleep compared to the respective single heterozygotes, suggesting that loss of neuropeptide signaling contributes to the aus sleep phenotype (p < 0.01; Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction experiments shown in Figure 4C with statistical significance p < 0.01

claim: CG16791 was previously identified as a protein that interacts with the cell engulfment receptor Draper
source: In investigating the mechanism by which aus regulates sleep, we noted that CG16791 was previously identified as a protein that interacts with the cell engulfment receptor Draper (Fullard and Baker, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited study

claim: Draper is involved in cell death associated with autophagy
source: Draper is involved in cell death associated with autophagy, the primary disposal pathway for large-scale cellular waste such as protein aggregates and damaged organelles, and an emergency nutrient source (McPhee et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited study

claim: Neither the number nor the size of all mCherry(+) puncta is significantly different in argus mutants compared to controls
source: Neither the number nor the size of all mCherry(+) puncta was significantly different in aus mutants compared to controls (p > 0.05; Figure 5B–C)
evidence: The claim is supported by autophagy flux measurements shown in Figure 5B-C with no significant difference (p > 0.05)

claim: The distribution of autophagy puncta in argus mutants is significantly skewed toward double-labeled puncta with a reduction in the number of mCherry-alone puncta
source: but the distribution was significantly skewed toward double-labeled puncta with a reduction in the number of mCherry-alone puncta, suggesting that inefficient lysosomal digestion drives autophagosome accumulation in aus mutants (p < 0.001; Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by autophagy flux measurements shown in Figure 5D with statistical significance p < 0.001

claim: Inefficient lysosomal digestion drives autophagosome accumulation in argus mutants
source: but the distribution was significantly skewed toward double-labeled puncta with a reduction in the number of mCherry-alone puncta, suggesting that inefficient lysosomal digestion drives autophagosome accumulation in aus mutants (p < 0.001; Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the autophagy flux measurements showing accumulation of autophagosomes relative to autolysosomes

claim: Rapamycin pre-treatment increases total mCherry(+) puncta compared to vehicle control
source: As expected, given its well-characterized role as a TOR inhibitor and inducer of starvation-dependent autophagy, rapamycin pre-treatment increased total mCherry(+) puncta compared to vehicle control, with no significant difference in either the size of these puncta or the ratio of mCherry+ GFP autophagosomes to mCherry-only autolysosomes (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by rapamycin treatment experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-D

claim: The blue cheese 58 loss-of-function allele increases sleep compared to iso31 control
source: We found that bchs increases sleep compared to iso31 control (p < 0.01), primarily by lengthening night sleep bouts (p < 0.001) (Figure 6A, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by sleep measurements shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C with statistical significance p < 0.01

claim: blue cheese decreases latency to sleep at nightfall
source: bchs also decreases latency to sleep at nightfall (p < 0.0001), suggesting that the sleep gain reflects increased sleep need (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by sleep latency measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D with statistical significance p < 0.0001

claim: The blue cheese mutant is best known for an autophagy defect that decreases the accumulation of autophagosomes and drives neurodegeneration
source: The bchs mutant is best known for an autophagy defect that decreases the accumulation of autophagosomes and drives neurodegeneration (Finley et al., 2003; Simonsen et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited studies

claim: A single allele of blue cheese robustly and non-additively suppresses sleep phenotypes of argus
source: While a single allele of bchs had no effect on total sleep amount compared to control iso31 (Figure 6A), it robustly and non-additively suppressed sleep phenotypes of aus, rendering the bchs/+; aus/+ transheterozygotes statistically indistinguishable from bchs/+ for total, day, and night sleep amount, all of which were higher than aus/+ (p < 0.05; Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction experiments shown in Figure 6B with statistical significance p < 0.05

claim: The blue cheese sleep phenotype is epistatic to that of argus
source: Our findings suggest that the bchs sleep phenotype is indeed epistatic to that of aus, consistent with their respective effects on the autophagy pathway.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic interaction experiments showing bchs suppression of aus phenotype

claim: Pan-neuronal atg5 RNAi increases sleep on an argus mutant background
source: Both pan-neuronal atg RNAis increased sleep on an aus mutant background (p < 0.05), driven selectively by increases in night sleep (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi rescue experiments shown in Figure 6C with statistical significance p < 0.05

claim: Pan-neuronal atg7 RNAi increases sleep on an argus mutant background
source: Both pan-neuronal atg RNAis increased sleep on an aus mutant background (p < 0.05), driven selectively by increases in night sleep (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi rescue experiments shown in Figure 6D with statistical significance p < 0.05

claim: atg7 RNAi decreases sleep in control flies lacking the argus mutation
source: Importantly, neither RNAi increased sleep in flies lacking the aus mutation—in fact, atg7 RNAi decreased sleep in control flies—indicating that the rescue of aus did not result from an additive interaction (p < 0.001; Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B with statistical significance p < 0.001

claim: atg5 and atg7 RNAi rescue the sleep defect of argus/+ flies
source: Much like the bchs mutant, atg5 and atg7 RNAi also rescue the milder sleep defect of aus/+ flies (p < 0.001; Figure 6—figure supplement 2E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi rescue experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2E,F with statistical significance p < 0.001

claim: Five RNAis for four genes significantly increased sleep in the pan-neuronal nsyb-geneswitch screen
source: We first screened with pan-neuronal nsyb-geneswitch+ uas-dicer on RU+ food, and identified five RNAis for four genes that significantly increased sleep (p < 0.05; Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi screen results shown in Figure 7A with statistical significance p < 0.05

claim: Atg1 RNAi knockdown increases sleep in the pan-neuronal nsyb-geneswitch screen
source: These included upstream regulators that couple autophagy to starvation (Atg1, 2 RNAi's), unfolded protein response (Bip), and ecdysone signaling (Daor) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B,D,E; Hale et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi screen results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: Bip RNAi knockdown increases sleep in the pan-neuronal nsyb-geneswitch screen
source: These included upstream regulators that couple autophagy to starvation (Atg1, 2 RNAi's), unfolded protein response (Bip), and ecdysone signaling (Daor) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B,D,E; Hale et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi screen results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D

claim: Daor RNAi knockdown increases sleep in the pan-neuronal nsyb-geneswitch screen
source: These included upstream regulators that couple autophagy to starvation (Atg1, 2 RNAi's), unfolded protein response (Bip), and ecdysone signaling (Daor) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B,D,E; Hale et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi screen results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E

claim: Atg10 RNAi knockdown increases sleep in the pan-neuronal nsyb-geneswitch screen
source: The remaining gain-of-sleep hit was Atg10, an E2 ligase-like enzyme involved in autophagosome vesicle expansion (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C; Hale et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi screen results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C

claim: The actin-geneswitch screen yielded more gain-of-sleep hits than the nsyb-geneswitch screen
source: To accomplish broad and strong knockdown of autophagy genes, we repeated the same screen with actin-geneswitch. As expected, this approach yielded more gain-of-sleep hits (P < 0.05; Figure 7B)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of screen results shown in Figure 7A and 7B

claim: Two distinct RNAis encoding Atg8b increase sleep in the actin-geneswitch screen
source: As expected, this approach yielded more gain-of-sleep hits (P < 0.05; Figure 7B), including several autophagosome maturation proteins: two distinct RNAis encoding Atg8b (one of two ubiquitin-like homologs that label mature autophagosomes), and single RNAis for Atg12 and Atg7 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1H,I,J,K; Hale et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi screen results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1I,J

claim: Atg12 RNAi knockdown increases sleep in the actin-geneswitch screen
source: As expected, this approach yielded more gain-of-sleep hits (P < 0.05; Figure 7B), including several autophagosome maturation proteins: two distinct RNAis encoding Atg8b (one of two ubiquitin-like homologs that label mature autophagosomes), and single RNAis for Atg12 and Atg7 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1H,I,J,K; Hale et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi screen results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1K

claim: Atg7 RNAi knockdown increases sleep in the actin-geneswitch screen
source: As expected, this approach yielded more gain-of-sleep hits (P < 0.05; Figure 7B), including several autophagosome maturation proteins: two distinct RNAis encoding Atg8b (one of two ubiquitin-like homologs that label mature autophagosomes), and single RNAis for Atg12 and Atg7 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1H,I,J,K; Hale et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi screen results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1H

claim: Both atg1 RNAi crosses increase total sleep
source: Both atg1 RNAi crosses increased total sleep (p < 0.0001; Figure 7C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by validation experiments shown in Figure 7C-D with statistical significance p < 0.0001

claim: nsybGS> dcr,atg1 RNAi#1 increases sleep largely RU-dependently
source: The nsybGS> dcr,atg1 RNAi#1 increased sleep largely RU-dependently, while nsybGS> dcr,atg1 RNAi#4 increased sleep largely RU-independently, suggesting a leaky GS/RNAi combination (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by drug-inducible RNAi experiments shown in Figure 7C

claim: nsybGS> dcr,atg1 RNAi#4 increases sleep largely RU-independently, suggesting a leaky GS/RNAi combination
source: The nsybGS> dcr,atg1 RNAi#1 increased sleep largely RU-dependently, while nsybGS> dcr,atg1 RNAi#4 increased sleep largely RU-independently, suggesting a leaky GS/RNAi combination (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by drug-inducible RNAi experiments shown in Figure 7D and inferred from the RU-independent effect

claim: Both atg1 RNAi crosses have consistently longer night and longest sleep bout lengths on RU+ food
source: But both atg1 RNAi crosses had many flies with massive single night-time sleep bouts, and on RU+ food we found consistently longer night (p < 0.01) and longest (p < 0.0001) sleep bout lengths, with significantly lower night bout number (p < 0.05), suggesting that consolidation of night sleep drives overall sleep gain in these flies (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B,C,G,H,I).
evidence: The claim is supported by sleep bout analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B,C,G,H,I with statistical significance p < 0.01 and p < 0.0001

claim: Consolidation of night sleep drives overall sleep gain in atg1 RNAi flies
source: But both atg1 RNAi crosses had many flies with massive single night-time sleep bouts, and on RU+ food we found consistently longer night (p < 0.01) and longest (p < 0.0001) sleep bout lengths, with significantly lower night bout number (p < 0.05), suggesting that consolidation of night sleep drives overall sleep gain in these flies (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B,C,G,H,I).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the sleep bout analysis showing longer bouts and fewer bout numbers

claim: Sleep latency at nightfall is consistently decreased in both atg1 RNAi crosses on both foods
source: Sleep latency at nightfall was consistently decreased in both atg1 RNAi crosses on both foods (p < 0.01), with an even stronger decrease on RU+ vs RU- (p < 0.001; Figure 7—figure supplement 2D,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by sleep latency measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2D,J with statistical significance p < 0.01

claim: Food-independent increased waking activity in atg1 knockdowns excludes the possibility that sleep increases are derived from sickness
source: Food-independent increased waking activity in atg1 knockdowns excludes the possibility that sleep increases are derived from sickness (p < 0.05; Figure 7—figure supplement 2E,K).
evidence: The claim is inferred from activity measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2E,K

claim: qPCR quantification confirmed knockdown of atg1 by RNAi alleles in actinGS> dcr,atg1 RNAi flies
source: Finally, qPCR quantification confirmed knockdown of atg1 by our RNAi alleles in actinGS> dcr,atg1 RNAi flies (p < 0.05; Figure 7—figure supplement 2F,L).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2F,L with statistical significance p < 0.05

claim: Both actinGS> dcr,atg8b RNAis robustly and RU-dependently increase night sleep
source: Both actinGS> dcr,atg8b RNAis robustly and RU-dependently increased night sleep, but only RNAi#2 increased total sleep and day sleep after back-crossing (Figure 7E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by validation experiments shown in Figure 7E-F

claim: Both atg8b RNAis RU-dependently increase mean sleep bout length
source: Both atg8b RNAis RU-dependently increased mean sleep bout length (p < 0.05), driven disproportionately by longest bout (p < 0.05; Figure 7—figure supplement 2M-O,S-U).
evidence: The claim is supported by sleep bout analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2M-O,S-U with statistical significance p < 0.05

claim: atg8b RNAis may effect their sleep gain by knockdown of atg8a through conserved sequences
source: As qPCR did not consistently detect atg8b even in control fly extracts, suggesting very low expression, atg8b RNAis may effect their sleep gain by knockdown of atg8a through conserved sequences. This was supported by qPCR quantification of atg8a cDNA in actinGS> dcr,atg8b RNAi flies (p < 0.05; Figure 7—figure supplement 2R,X).
evidence: The claim is inferred from qPCR results showing atg8a knockdown by atg8b RNAi, shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2R,X

claim: Pan-neuronal atg1 and whole-fly atg8 knockdown phenotypes largely recapitulate the key hallmarks of blue cheese phenotypes
source: In sum, pan-neuronal atg1 and whole-fly atg8 knockdown phenotypes largely recapitulate the key hallmarks of bchs phenotypes: (1) sleep gain disproportionately driven by night sleep, (2) sleep consolidation, and (3) decreased sleep latency at nightfall (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of RNAi phenotypes with bchs phenotypes

claim: RU-dependence of many phenotypes demonstrates that perturbing autophagosome formation in adulthood is sufficient to drive changes in sleep
source: RU-dependence of many phenotypes demonstrates that perturbing autophagosome formation in adulthood is sufficient to drive changes in sleep.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the drug-inducible RNAi experiments showing adult-specific effects

claim: In the early night, there are more total mCherry(+) puncta than in the early day
source: In the early night, there were more total mCherry(+) puncta than in the early day, with no significant difference in the size of mCherry(+) puncta or the ratio of mCherry+ GFP autophagosomes to mCherry-only autolysosomes, suggesting a potential role for sleep:wake state in regulating the production of autophagosomes (p < 0.05; Figure 8B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by autophagy flux measurements at different times shown in Figure 8B with statistical significance p < 0.05

claim: Sleep deprivation increases total mCherry(+) puncta compared to controls at ZT0-2
source: SD flies had significantly more total mCherry(+) puncta compared to controls, with no significant difference in the size of mCherry(+) puncta or the ratio of mCherry+ GFP autophagosomes to mCherry-only autolysosomes (Figure 8F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by sleep deprivation experiments shown in Figure 8F

claim: Gaboxadol treatment markedly increases sleep
source: As previously reported, gaboxadol treatment markedly increased sleep (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E; Berry et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by gaboxadol treatment experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1E and cited studies

claim: Gaboxadol flies have significantly fewer total mCherry(+) puncta compared to controls
source: Gaboxadol flies had significantly fewer total mCherry(+) puncta compared to controls, with no significant difference in either the size of mCherry(+) puncta or the ratio of mCherry+ GFP autophagosomes to mCherry-only autolysosomes (Figure 8J–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by gaboxadol treatment experiments shown in Figure 8J

claim: Wake increases and sleep decreases autophagosome number in wild-type fly neurons
source: These data showing that wake increases and sleep decreases autophagosome number in wild-type fly neurons (Figure 8) were unexpected because they could be interpreted as sleep-promotion by autophagosomes, while our mutant and RNAi data indicate that high neuronal autophagosome number decreases sleep and low neuronal autophagosome number promotes sleep (Figures 1 and 5—7).
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined results from Figure 8 showing time-of-day, sleep deprivation, and gaboxadol effects on autophagosome levels

claim: High neuronal autophagosome number decreases sleep
source: These data showing that wake increases and sleep decreases autophagosome number in wild-type fly neurons (Figure 8) were unexpected because they could be interpreted as sleep-promotion by autophagosomes, while our mutant and RNAi data indicate that high neuronal autophagosome number decreases sleep and low neuronal autophagosome number promotes sleep (Figures 1 and 5—7).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the argus mutant phenotype showing autophagosome accumulation and sleep loss

claim: Low neuronal autophagosome number promotes sleep
source: These data showing that wake increases and sleep decreases autophagosome number in wild-type fly neurons (Figure 8) were unexpected because they could be interpreted as sleep-promotion by autophagosomes, while our mutant and RNAi data indicate that high neuronal autophagosome number decreases sleep and low neuronal autophagosome number promotes sleep (Figures 1 and 5—7).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the bchs mutant and atg RNAi phenotypes showing reduced autophagosome formation and sleep gain

claim: The phenotypes of the mutants/RNAis reflect sustained high or low levels of autophagosomes not seen during a normal daily cycle
source: As discussed below, we believe that the phenotypes of the mutants/RNAis reflect sustained high or low levels of autophagosomes not seen during a normal daily cycle (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is speculated based on the authors' interpretation of their data

claim: Drosophila is a powerful model for the use of unbiased approaches to identify the molecular basis of a physiological process of interest
source: Drosophila is a powerful model for the use of unbiased approaches to identify the molecular basis of a physiological process of interest.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Drosophila as a model organism

claim: The molecular basis of the circadian clock was determined largely through forward genetic screens
source: Indeed, the molecular basis of the circadian clock was determined largely through forward genetic screens of the type used to isolate aus (Dubowy and Sehgal, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited review

claim: The argus sleep mutant is unique in that the mechanisms underlying its loss of sleep are likely relevant for sleep function
source: The aus sleep mutant is unique, in that the mechanisms underlying its loss of sleep are likely relevant for sleep function (discussed below).
evidence: The claim is speculated based on the authors' interpretation of their findings

claim: argus is temporally elevated during the embryo cellularization and late larval/early pupal stages of fruit fly development
source: aus is temporally elevated during the embryo cellularization and late larval / early pupal stages of fruit fly development, times of enhanced developmental autophagy.
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data from cited databases

claim: High autophagy during late larval/early pupal stage provided the first observation of the autophagy pathway in Drosophila melanogaster
source: Indeed, high autophagy during the latter stage provided the first observation of the pathway in Drosophila melanogaster (Kuhn et al., 2015; Thurmond et al., 2019; Gaudecker, 1963).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited historical studies

claim: argus expression is spatially enriched in tissues with high levels of developmental and adult autophagy, including brain, gut, and fat body
source: aus expression is also spatially enriched in tissues with high levels of developmental and adult autophagy, including brain, gut, and fat body (Thurmond et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data from a cited database

claim: The cell membrane, endoplasmic reticulum, and Golgi apparatus cellular compartments are all proposed donors of autophagosome membranes
source: Finally, this hypothesis is consistent with our bioinformatic predictions, as the cell membrane, endoplasmic reticulum, and Golgi apparatus cellular compartments are all proposed donors of autophagosome membranes (Supplementary file 2; Nishimura and Tooze, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic predictions and a cited study

claim: Argus is required for transition of autophagosomes to autolysosomes
